extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and educated readers interested in evaluating or producing fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding criteria for evaluating and producing modern fiction (especially novels and short stories) with attention to authenticity, political/democratic sentiment, genre choice (realism vs melodrama), and the relation of art to doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background authenticity (localness vs transplanted metropolitan sensibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: When colonial or provincial writers write most sincerely and successfully, their work should arise from a genuine local background rather than from an assumed metropolitan background: 'when they write most sincerely and most successfully, it is not with a background of the mystery of the bush, but with a background... of our own romantic cockney civilization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work genuinely springs from local experience or merely transposes metropolitan attitudes and atmospheres. Note exceptions (e.g., Olive Schreiner) where authentic non-English sensibility produces genuine originality. Anti-pattern: colonial fiction that only imitates English urban romance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary novelty — 'a new book' vs repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A culture or colony should be judged by whether it has produced truly new literature: 'they have not given the world a new book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work contributes a genuinely new vision or merely repeats existing tropes. It is acceptable to evoke new emotions, but that is not the same as producing a new literary form or insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as a test of national vitality (heroic art)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief signs of a nation's being 'glad and great' is the heroic in art: 'There are three main shapes or symbols in which a nation can show itself essentially glad and great—by the heroic in government, by the heroic in arms, and by the heroic in art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge national or cultural literature by whether its art displays heroism, seriousness, and a public-spirited grandeur rather than mere novelty or polish. Works that reflect only private refinement without public or heroic dimension may signal cultural decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic signs of vitality versus decadence
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of great artists in a culture is not automatically evidence of vitality; it may indicate 'a fine futility and the end of all things': 'out of America has come a sweet and startling cry, as unmistakable as the cry of a dying man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating major artists, consider whether their work points to creative youthfulness or to terminal refinement/decadence. Great technical achievement can coexist with cultural exhaustion; differentiate energetic innovation from elegiac mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic emotion (reverence for the common man)
rubrics_metrics.description: True democratic sentiment in literature is an instinctive reverence for the common man and an emphasis on shared human essentials: 'the democratic emotion... feels the things in which all men agree to be unspeakably important, and all the things in which they differ... to be almost unspeakably unimportant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that treat ordinary humanity with reverence rather than pity or condescension. Watch for portrayals that reduce the poor to objects of pity or study rather than fellow human beings; democratic art honours common humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination/empathy over 'studying' poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic writer should imagine and identify with the poor rather than 'study' them as exotic subjects: 'my first objection to him will be that he has studied his subject. A democrat would have imagined it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer portrayals arising from imaginative empathy rather than detached sociological observation. Anti-pattern: writers who treat poverty as an anthropological curiosity or merely collect details to astonish readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'artistic slumming' (exploitation of the poor for impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic slumming—taking up poor people merely for impressions or copy—is condemned: 'The most despicable of all is artistic slumming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish honest impression-seeking (sensational aims declared as such) from exploitative claims to represent the spiritual core of the poor. If a writer seeks only shocking detail without moral seriousness or authentic perspective, mark it as slumming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and temporal perspective (journalist vs missionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers differ in the temporal authority of their claims: the journalist gives a day-to-day version, while the missionary (an 'eternalist') claims a version that holds for all time: 'the journalist is... a journalist, while the missionary is an eternalist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a novelist claims to represent the 'spiritual core' or eternal condition of a class, evaluate whether the author has the authority and outlook to justify such claims. Anti-pattern: journalists or reporters posing as eternal interpreters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-standpoint authenticity (the writer's class colors portrayal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slum fiction often reflects the psychology of the writer's class encountering poverty rather than the psychology of poverty itself: 'these books are a record of the psychology of wealth and culture when brought in contact with poverty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the author's social position shapes the depiction. Look for whether details function to astonish the (middle-class) reader rather than to illuminate the lived reality of the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-fit: realism vs melodrama in truth-telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Realistic stories may be more artistically refined, but melodrama can be 'much more like life'—especially the life of the poor, who are naturally melodramatic: 'the melodrama is much more like man, and especially the poor man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically privilege realism as the only truthful mode. Consider whether melodramatic conventions (heightened emotion, explicit moral maxims) better capture the subject's lived truth. Anti-pattern: dismissing melodrama as merely 'inartistic' when it may be more faithful to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation as a legitimate aesthetic aim
rubrics_metrics.description: If novels about slums are intended to be sensational, that can be 'a noble and reasonable object'—a shock or sensation can be a valid aesthetic goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sensational works by whether they achieve their declared aesthetic aims (to shock, to provoke) honestly and effectively, rather than assuming sensationalism is inherently low or dishonest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogmatism and definite convictions in writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental and artistic progress should lead to definite convictions; 'Man can be defined as an animal that makes dogmas... no man ought to write at all... unless he thinks that he is in truth and the other man in error.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize writers who write with conviction and a constructive philosophy of life. Assess whether the writer has coherent, affirmative doctrines rather than cultivated scepticism or vague broad-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of art and doctrine — artists as doctrinaires/propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the boldest modern artists have been 'doctrinaires' who write 'with a purpose'; strong doctrines often produce startling art: 'the men who have really been the bold artists... are the men who have turned out... to be writing "with a purpose."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art, consider the relationship between artistic quality and the author's doctrinal purpose. Doctrinaire intent can enrich art; distinguish honest didacticism from mere propagandistic dullness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting the 'aspects of truth' evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissing conflicting positions as merely different 'aspects of truth' can be an evasion: 'this seems to me an evasion which has not even had the sense to disguise itself ingeniously in words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of critics or artists who neutralize disagreement by calling all competing views 'aspects'—demand clarity about truth-claims and whether the work asserts or denies particular truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge art with regard to the artist's convictions and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not enjoy or judge a work in isolation from its author's aims and convictions: 'No man has any right whatever merely to enjoy the work of Mr. Bernard Shaw; he might as well enjoy the invasion of his country by the French.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a work is overtly political or doctrinal, evaluate it both aesthetically and ethically/politically. Recognize that appreciation divorced from awareness of the author's aims can be a kind of complicity or error.
